core: Working definition of electrolytes: minerals that carry an electric charge when dissolved in water or body fluids such as blood (attributed to MedlinePlus and Merck Manual)

The main electrolytes, each with one line: sodium (fluid, nerves, muscles), potassium (cells, heart, muscles), chloride (fluid, blood volume/pressure), calcium (bones, teeth, muscles, nerves), magnesium (muscles, nerves, heart, many processes)
What they do, each named with one line: nerve signals, muscle contraction, fluid balance
How the body keeps balance: healthy kidneys keep the right balance of electrolytes in the blood (stated simply)

Losing and replacing: sweat and illness (vomiting/diarrhea) remove electrolytes; food and drink replace them; the honest note that sports drinks are mainly for intense exercise, not everyday activity (no marketing)
Food sources: table salt (sodium and chloride), fruits (potassium), vegetables (potassium and magnesium), dairy (calcium, potassium, magnesium)
Honest framing: electrolytes are the body's electrical crew; balance, not more, is the goal
supporting: An electrolyte imbalance means the level of one or more electrolytes is too low or too high
Common causes of imbalance: severe vomiting and/or diarrhea, heavy sweating, not drinking enough fluids, certain medicines, kidney problems
Electrolytes keep the heart rate and rhythm steady and help keep blood pressure stable
Almost all of the body's calcium is stored in bones and teeth
Most dietary sodium comes from salt that is in or added to food

claims.claim: Electrolytes are minerals that have an electric charge when they are dissolved in water or body fluids, including blood; the charge can be positive or negative.

The main electrolytes in the body include sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, and magnesium; sodium helps control the amount of fluid in the body and helps nerves and muscles work properly, potassium helps cells, the heart, and muscles work properly, chloride helps control fluid and helps maintain healthy blood volume and blood pressure, calcium helps make and keep bones and teeth strong, and magnesium helps muscles, nerves, and the heart work properly.
Electrolytes help balance the amount of water in the body, support muscle and nerve function, keep the heart rate and rhythm steady, and help keep blood pressure stable.

Potassium is needed for proper kidney and heart function, muscle contraction, and nerve transmission; calcium is needed for muscles to move and for nerves to carry messages; magnesium regulates muscle and nerve function.
Healthy kidneys keep the right balance of electrolytes in the blood.

An electrolyte imbalance means the level of one or more electrolytes in the body is too low or too high; common causes include severe vomiting and/or diarrhea, heavy sweating, not drinking enough fluids, certain medicines, and heart, liver, or kidney problems.
Electrolytes are lost from the body in sweat and in large amounts through vomiting and diarrhea; you get electrolytes from the foods you eat and the fluids you drink.

Hydration drinks containing electrolytes, sugar, and caffeine (sports drinks) may be helpful after intense exercise in adults but are not typically needed for everyday activity; the more vigorous and longer the exercise, the more evidence supports rehydration beverages with carbohydrates and electrolytes.
Table salt supplies sodium and chloride; most dietary sodium comes from salt that is in or added to food, and the body needs salt (which contains sodium) to work properly.

Fruits such as bananas, dried apricots, prunes, raisins, and orange juice and vegetables such as potatoes, spinach, tomatoes, and broccoli are rich sources of potassium; milk and yogurt provide calcium (and also potassium and magnesium); legumes, nuts, seeds, and green leafy vegetables are good sources of magnesium.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do most people need sports drinks to replace electrolytes lost in exercise?
positions: Marketing and common belief: after any workout that produces sweat, a sports drink is needed to replace lost electrolytes.

Evidence: electrolyte/sports drinks may be helpful after intense exercise in adults but are not typically needed for everyday activity; food and water replace routine losses (OpenStax nutrition text; MedlinePlus notes electrolytes come from foods and fluids).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the evidence-based position and does not recommend products: ordinary activity is covered by food and water, and sports drinks are a choice for long or intense exercise.

positions: Common assumption: extra electrolytes provide extra benefit, so supplementation or heavy use of electrolyte drinks is desirable.
Evidence: an electrolyte imbalance means a level is too low OR too high; treatment depends on which electrolyte and which direction, and healthy kidneys regulate levels (MedlinePlus; Merck Manual).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents balance as the goal, not surplus, and notes that both too little and too much cause problems.
